narrative: The model estimated your chance of failing the bar exam on the first attempt at 62.9%, meaning failure was considered more likely than passing; on that basis, your law-school application was denied. The decision did not rely on your gender or race. The strongest influence was your undergraduate GPA of 3.70, which is above the 3.23 average for accepted students. This factor worked in your favor and pushed the prediction toward passing. However, the next two most important factors were your third-year class-standing measure and then your first-year class-standing measure, and both pushed the prediction toward failure. Your values on those measures were 1, while accepted students averaged about 5.8 to 6.0; despite that comparison, the model still treated these standing measures as risk factors in your case. Together, those two risk factors outweighed the benefit of your GPA and led to the denial. To improve a future application, meet an admissions adviser, ask what evidence would offset the model's concern, strengthen your academic record if possible, consider retaking the LSAT (22 versus an accepted average of 37.18), and document any bar-exam preparation or support plan before reapplying.
